Turf for Dundee Pool Cages and Screened Lanais

Turf beside a screened Dundee pool prices the same as any residential lawn, $8–$18 a square foot, and it's the ridge's open, full-sun exposure, more than the pool water itself, that decides how that turf has to be built. A strip inside a lanai over existing concrete needs a drainage layer the surrounding yard doesn't, whether the house sits downtown or on a new Woodland Ranch Estates lot.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Why a lanai deck needs its own drainage layer

Turf laid inside a screened pool cage almost always sits on an existing concrete deck rather than bare soil, and concrete doesn't drain the way a washed-rock base does, so a drainage underlay goes between the slab and the turf backing to give rinse water and rain somewhere to go besides sitting on top of the concrete. The perimeter gets glued rather than staked, since there's no soil at the deck's edge for a nail to grip, and that glued bond is usually the first thing to check after a season of pool splash-out and hose rinsing. None of this changes with a house's location in Dundee; a lanai on a ridge lot and one two blocks from Lake Marie get the same deck treatment.

Full sun on an open ridge lot versus a shaded in-town yard

Away from Dundee's older, tree-lined blocks, a lot on open ridge ground can leave a pool deck and its surrounding turf in full sun most of the day, the same exposure a crew sees on similar ridge lots toward Lake Alfred and Davenport, which pushes surface temperatures well past what the same turf would reach under an oak canopy near the depot. A hose rinse drops that temperature 30 to 50 degrees within minutes, which matters more around a pool deck than almost anywhere else in the yard, since bare feet cross it constantly between the water and a lounge chair. A lighter-colored infill or a planned shade sail over part of the deck both help on a lot that doesn't have mature trees to lean on yet.

Why washed rock matters most where concrete meets soil

Rainfall that hits a pool deck's concrete has nowhere to go but sideways, onto whatever soil border sits at the cage's edge, so a Dundee lot's washed, open-graded crushed rock does more work at that transition than it does in the middle of an open lawn. Unwashed fill would let fines settle and bind right where the extra volume arrives first, turning a narrow strip into the one part of the yard that stays soggy after every storm. The state's rule that subgrade material be washed before installation exists for exactly this kind of concentrated flow, not just ordinary rain falling evenly across a yard.

Letting the adhesive cure before the pool goes back into use

Glued seams and perimeter adhesive on a Dundee lanai floor need time to set before anyone walks the surface, and that cure window matters more here than on a soil job because a pool deck stays humid and occasionally wet even when it is not actively raining. Foot traffic across a seam before the adhesive has fully bonded can shift the join enough to open a gap later, and a splash from the pool itself while the glue is still curing does the same thing rainfall would to an unfinished soil job. Scheduling the last coat early in the day gives it hours of dry cure before evening pool use resumes.

Say you have a 300 sq ft strip around a Dundee pool cage

Say a resurfaced pool on an older Dundee lot has a 300 sq ft ring of bare dirt and dead grass between the deck and the screen enclosure's frame. At $8–$18 a square foot, that strip prices between $2,400 and $5,400 installed, with the deck's own drainage underlay pushing toward the higher end and a simple soil-based strip along the outside of the cage pushing toward the lower one. The same strip on a new Woodland Ranch Estates pool home prices identically per square foot, since the deck's construction, not the neighborhood, sets where in that range a specific job lands.

Choosing infill that won't wash toward the deck drain

The state's rule against infill washing off the property has a specific practical version on a Dundee pool deck: infill brushed in too lightly along a border that slopes toward the deck's drain can wash into that drain during a hard rinse or a storm, which turns a turf maintenance issue into a plumbing one. A slightly heavier grain of whichever infill the border uses, silica or coated sand, resists that migration better than a lighter, finer product does in exactly this drain-facing situation. This is a narrower concern than general odor or bacteria control, and it only applies to the specific stretch of border actually sloping toward a drain.

Keeping capped irrigation clear of a pool equipment pad

A pool equipment pad usually sits close to whatever irrigation zone used to water that side of the house, and capping those heads at the valve box, required once turf goes down, needs to happen without blocking access to the pump and filter housing later. On an older Dundee lot that equipment pad is often original to the pool's installation decades ago; on a new Woodland Ranch Estates build, it's recent enough that the irrigation plan and the pool equipment layout were at least drawn on the same site plan. Either way, marking the pad's service clearance before finalizing where turf and its edging go avoids a callback to move something that should have stayed put.

Keeping a shaded pool corner outside an oak's root zone

A mature oak shading part of a Dundee pool deck sounds like the ideal spot for turf that stays cooler through the afternoon, but the drip-line rule applies here exactly as it does anywhere else on the lot: no turf inside the canopy's root zone without a certified arborist's letter confirming the install will not harm the tree. Digging even a shallow lanai-floor edge or a border's rock base near exposed surface roots close to the trunk can do real damage before anyone notices. Getting that letter before committing to a shaded layout is the only way to use the space legally.

Rechecking a septic lid's clearance years after a pool project

A septic lid marked and protected during a Dundee pool-area turf build is worth rechecking periodically in the years afterward, since new landscaping, a stored pool float, or equipment added near the pump pad over time can gradually encroach on a spot nobody's paying close attention to anymore. Confirming the lid is still visible and clear takes only a minute during any other routine check of the border or lanai floor, and it's far easier than rediscovering the location from scratch the day a pump-out truck actually needs it. This matters most on properties where the original construction notes have long since been forgotten.

Questions people ask

Does turf around a Dundee pool need a different infill because of chlorine splash-out?

No infill change is needed for chlorine specifically. Silica sand or coated sand both hold up fine against occasional splash-out; the bigger consideration around a pool deck is the drainage underlay under the turf, not the infill on top of it.

Is a shaded in-town pool lanai cooler than one on an open ridge lot?

Usually, yes, if mature trees actually block direct sun for part of the day. Surface temperature is the main difference; the turf construction, drainage layer and glued edges over the concrete deck, stays the same regardless of how much shade a specific Dundee lot gets.
